explanations.explanation: Jesus saw Levi sitting at his tax booth and told him, "Follow Me." Just two words. No speech, no list of rules first. Levi, a tax collector, got an invitation before he got anything else.

I can see why you'd think that, since tax collectors didn't have the best name around town. But the text has Jesus say something much shorter. He tells Levi, "Follow Me," and that's the whole invitation. Nothing about repaying is in these verses.

That line is tucked in another story in the Bible, so I get the mix-up. Here, Jesus sees Levi at the tax booth and says, "Follow Me." That's all the text gives us. Short and simple, like a note on the fridge.
Levi "got up, left everything, and followed Him." No stalling, no "let me check my calendar." The text says he left everything, and I'd have a hard time leaving a counter full of warm dough.

explanations.answer: Asks to finish his day first
explanations.explanation: That sounds like most of us on a Monday, doesn't it? "Just let me wrap up a few things." But the text doesn't have Levi ask for anything. He got up, left everything and followed Jesus.

I bet plenty of us would ask that one out loud. Levi doesn't, though. The text says he "got up, left everything, and followed Him." No questions are written down, just a man getting up from his booth.
Luke says "a large crowd of tax collectors was there." Levi was a tax collector himself, so his guest list was folks he knew. Bring your own coworkers to the party and you get the same crowd.

Fishermen show up in Luke's Gospel just before this passage, so I see how they stuck in your head. At Levi's banquet, though, the text says a large crowd of tax collectors was there. Nobody mentions a single fishing net at that table.

Soldiers do turn up around tax collectors elsewhere in Luke, but not at this table. Levi's banquet had "a large crowd of tax collectors," along with others who were eating with them. I think the soldiers were busy somewhere else that night.

Close, but the text adds a little more. A large crowd of tax collectors was there, "along with others who were eating with them." So the guest list had more than tax collectors. Levi's table had room for everybody.

Yep. The text says a large crowd of tax collectors was there, "along with others who were eating with them." So there were people at that table who weren't tax collectors. It was a full house, and I love a full house.

explanations.answer: Eating with tax collectors and sinners
explanations.explanation: The Pharisees and their scribes ask, "Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?" They bring the complaint to the disciples, not straight to Jesus. It's the kind of question you ask while looking at the guest list.

That complaint does come up with the Pharisees in other places, so you're not far off. But here the question is about the table. They ask, "Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?" Healing isn't mentioned in these verses.

Nothing in this passage says a word about sacrifices. The complaint is about who is sitting at the table. The Pharisees and their scribes ask, "Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?"

Jesus flips it around. He says, "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick." So the healthy part is the opposite of what He said. Nobody books a checkup because they feel great, except maybe me for the free lollipop.
Right. Jesus says, "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick." The doctor goes where the sick are. And He's answering the complaint about who He's eating with.

Jesus says, "I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance." He's still answering the complaint about His dinner guests. The call goes to the very folks the Pharisees were pointing at.
I can see why that word came to mind, since the Pharisees were pretty ready to hand it out. But Jesus says He has come to call sinners "to repentance." Judgment isn't the word He uses in this verse.
Service is a good word, but it isn't the one Jesus picks. He says, "I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance." Repentance is the end of that sentence.

The Pharisees and scribes say, "John's disciples and those of the Pharisees frequently fast and pray, but Yours keep on eating and drinking." John, remember, is John the Baptist. They're comparing the two groups side by side, like a stats chart at the break room.
Healing is something Jesus does a lot in Luke, but it isn't in their complaint. They say His disciples "keep on eating and drinking." It's all about the table again.
Ha, that would be a different complaint. The text has them say that Jesus' disciples "keep on eating and drinking." Nobody mentions naps in these verses.

Jesus asks, "Can you make the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them?" The picture is a wedding, and the bridegroom is right there with His guests. Nobody hands out a diet plan at that party.

It's an understandable guess, but Jesus isn't talking about leaving. He asks, "Can you make the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them?" The question comes right after they brought up fasting.

Work does sound like the opposite of a party. But the question follows the talk about fasting, so Jesus asks, "Can you make the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them?" The answer is in the question they just raised.

Jesus says, "the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast." The words are plain, and I think they're a heavy thing to hear. He says it quietly, right in the middle of an answer about a wedding.

It's a hard thing to hear, so I get wanting it to be false. But Jesus says, "the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast." That's what the text says, word for word.
Jesus says the opposite. If someone does that, "the patch from the new will not match the old." So the new garment gets torn and the patch still doesn't fit. That's a double loss.
Yes! Jesus says the new garment gets torn, and "the patch from the new will not match the old." So you ruin the new one and the old one still looks off. I've had cookie days like that.

explanations.answer: The skins burst and the wine spills
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, "the new wine will burst the skins, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined." Wineskins were containers for wine. Old ones can't handle the new, and everything ends up on the floor.

Jesus doesn't say anything about the wine changing. He says the new wine "will burst the skins, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined." It's about the skins giving out, not the wine aging.

explanations.answer: The skins stretch and hold it
explanations.explanation: That would be a happy ending, but it's not the one Jesus gives. He says, "the new wine will burst the skins, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined." Nothing stretches. It all goes wrong at once.
Jesus says, "new wine is poured into new wineskins." New goes with new. It's the plain fix to the problem He just described.
Old is the very thing that went wrong a moment ago. Jesus says, "no one pours new wine into old wineskins," and then, "Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins." Old skins are the problem.
Borrowed skins might be handy if you're short on cash, but Jesus doesn't mention them. He says, "new wine is poured into new wineskins." Just new and new.
Jesus says, "no one after drinking old wine wants new, for he says, 'The old is better.'" It's a simple picture of how comfortable the old can feel. A favorite recipe does that to me.
Jesus says the opposite. "No one after drinking old wine wants new." The person drinking old wine isn't reaching for the new, and he says, "The old is better."
